%1$s at a heat number of %2$s
%1$s for you · %2$s at a heat number of %3$s

Normal under 30°, Warm from 30°, Hot from 32°, Very hot from 35°, Extreme from 38°, judged on the whole number shown, so 31.5 shows as 32° and is Hot. Steps at 30, 32 and 34 borrow VTHC\'s rest table; 35 and 38 borrow workplace rules that use BOM shade air. HeatShield applies them to the heat number, which is never below air, so humid days reach each level sooner.
Heat number %1$s at %2$s

The higher of air temperature and feels like, so HeatShield never shows a heat number below the forecast air temperature. WorkSafe Vic: air temperature alone can\'t tell you the risk; humidity, sun, the work and clothing all count.
Heat number %1$s now (the hour from %2$s)
This hour\'s forecast, worked out the same way as the shift peak.
Feels like %1$s in shade · air %2$s at %3$s
BOM\'s shade formula, applied to the Open-Meteo forecast\'s air temperature, humidity and wind. In direct sun it can feel up to about 8° hotter.
Raised to %1$s for you

WorkSafe Vic and Safe Work Australia list hard physical work, heavy protective clothing and not being used to the heat (new, or back after time away) as risk factors. On Warm days and hotter, HeatShield adds one level for each, two at most.
At Extreme, HeatShield says stop heavy work outdoors. Its 38° step borrows workplace rules that read BOM shade air: Banyule tells outdoor staff to stop outdoor work above 38°.

An example threshold from workplace rules (AWU construction clause 35°, Banyule 38°), read from BOM shade air. Confirm the number with your team leader. HeatShield counts your shift hours where forecast air, in whole degrees, reaches %1$s. Crew rules usually go by a BOM reading on the day, not this forecast.

The number you set in Profile. Confirm it with your team leader. HeatShield counts your shift hours where forecast air, in whole degrees, reaches %1$s. Crew rules usually go by a BOM reading on the day, not this forecast.

Safe Work Australia and WorkSafe Vic advise doing physically demanding work in the cooler part of the day; heat stress is still possible early. HeatShield\'s cut-off is the first shift hour that would be Hot for heavy work, or that reaches your rule.

Low 0 to 2, Moderate 3 to 5, High 6 to 7, Very high 8 to 10, Extreme 11 and over. Sun protection starts at UV 3. Both are judged on the UV index as the whole number BOM reports, so a clear-sky forecast of 2.5 counts as 3.
Outdoor workers need sun protection all year
WorkSafe Vic: outdoor workers should use sun protection all year round to cut cumulative UV, and it is recommended whenever UV is 3 or more. SunSmart says the same for outdoor work.
Break suggestions need a current forecast.
No break suggestion at Normal heat

No regulator sets a break interval. HeatShield suggests: Warm, 60 min work then 10 min break; Hot, 45 then 15; Very hot, 30 then 15. At Extreme it suggests no work and break split: stop heavy work outdoors, and if your crew keeps working, take breaks in the shade and follow your crew\'s rule.
Union starting point: 15 min rest an hour from 30°, 30 from 32°, 45 from 34°, no work from 36°
VTHC\'s suggested place to start negotiating rest breaks. Ask your HSR what your crew has agreed.
Under 1 h old is fresh. Older than 6 h, or not covering today, it\'s marked out of date and break alerts pause until it updates.

Why this suggestion?
It uses today\'s forecast heat for your park and today\'s work: the shift you\'re running, your saved plan, or your usual day. Your crew\'s hot-day rule still applies.
